---
title: "Observability"
description: "The ability to understand a system's internal behavior from the outputs it exposes, such as logs, metrics, and traces."
term: "Observability"
letter: "O"
category: "MLOps"
difficulty: "Intermediate"
---

## Simple explanation

Observability helps an engineering team work out what a running system is
doing and why it may be behaving unexpectedly. Logs, metrics, and traces
provide different views of that behavior.

## Technical explanation

In software operations, logs record events, metrics summarize measurements
over time, and traces connect spans across a request's path through
services. ML observability may also track model inputs and outputs,
latency, errors, data quality, drift indicators, and task-specific
performance, subject to privacy and retention controls.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

A model can appear healthy at the infrastructure level while its input
distribution or output quality degrades. Observability supports incident
investigation, reliability work, and model monitoring, but it does not
replace a sound evaluation process or establish why a model made a
particular prediction.

## How it works

Instrument applications and services to emit structured telemetry, collect
it in a backend, and connect it to dashboards and alerts. For ML systems,
choose signals tied to user outcomes and operational risks, and avoid
logging sensitive content unless there is a justified, protected need.

## Practical example

For an inference API, a team could track request rate, error rate, latency
percentiles, and model version. A trace can show whether a slow response
came from feature retrieval, model inference, or another dependency.

## Common misconceptions

- Observability is not just collecting logs; useful signals need context and a way to investigate them.
- Monitoring dashboards do not automatically identify root cause.
- Capturing all model inputs can create privacy, security, and storage risks.
